toxins.name: Aromatic monoterpenes (thymol, p-cymene, carvacrol)
toxins.description: Monarda citriodora is not listed as toxic to cats by the ASPCA and is broadly regarded as non-toxic. Its lemon scent comes from aromatic monoterpenes — the essential oil is dominated by thymol, p-cymene, and carvacrol. It does NOT contain pulegone, menthol, or citrus compounds; pulegone is the toxic principle of pennyroyal (Mentha pulegium), a different plant. As with any plant, eating a large amount of leaf or stem material may cause mild, self-limiting stomach upset.
toxins.concentration_notes: No authoritative source documents serious systemic toxicity, hepatotoxicity, or a dangerous compound for this plant in cats. The only realistic concern is mild gastrointestinal irritation from eating plant material.

symptoms.name: Vomiting, Diarrhea, Nausea, Drooling (Hypersalivation)
symptoms.onset: Clinical signs typically appear shortly after ingestion (acute).
symptoms.notes: Mild, self-limiting stomach upset is possible after a cat eats plant material, as with many non-toxic plants. Drooling can occur as a reaction to the strong aromatic taste. This is not specific toxicity and no authoritative source documents serious effects from this plant.

symptoms.name: Skin Redness, Itching, Contact Dermatitis
symptoms.notes: Hypersensitive cats may occasionally develop mild skin irritation or redness around the mouth and paws after contact with the plant's aromatic oils. This is plausible but not specifically documented for this plant by authoritative sources.

treatments.name: Induction of Emesis (Vomiting) or Gastric Lavage (Stomach Pumping)
treatments.description: If the ingestion is recent, the veterinarian may administer medication to induce vomiting, effectively removing the plant material from the stomach before the toxins are fully absorbed. In more extreme cases, or if the cat cannot vomit safely, the vet may perform a gastric lavage (pumping the stomach) to wash out the contents.
treatments.notes: You should never attempt to induce vomiting at home (e.g., using hydrogen peroxide) without specific veterinary instruction, as this can cause further injury or complications. This procedure is most effective when performed shortly after ingestion.Toxin Adsorption (Activated Charcoal)

treatments.name: Administration of Activated Charcoal
treatments.description: Following decontamination, the veterinarian may administer activated charcoal. This substance works by binding to the remaining toxins in the gastrointestinal tract, preventing them from entering the bloodstream.
treatments.notes: This step is often taken if the vet suspects that toxins remain in the system after vomiting has been induced.

treatments.name: Fluid Support / Rehydration
treatments.description: The administration of IV fluids is used to stabilize the cat, correct dehydration caused by excessive vomiting or diarrhea, and help flush toxins from the body.
treatments.notes: This is critical if the cat has become dehydrated or if there is a risk of liver or kidney stress from the volatile oils found in the plant.Symptomatic Medication (Gastroprotectants and Anti-emetics)

treatments.name: Anti-nausea Medication and Antacids
treatments.description: To manage ongoing symptoms, the veterinarian may give an injection to stop nausea (anti-emetic) and administer medications to coat and soothe the stomach lining (gastric protectants/antacids).
treatments.notes: This is part of supportive care to keep the cat comfortable while they recover from the gastrointestinal irritation caused by the mint and citrus oils.

name: Lemon Mint
description: Lemon Mint (Monarda citriodora), also known as lemon beebalm, is a fragrant herb in the mint family (Lamiaceae) that is generally considered safe for cats. Despite its common name it is not a true mint (Mentha): it is not listed as toxic by the ASPCA, and its lemony scent comes from aromatic oils dominated by thymol, p-cymene, and carvacrol — it does not contain pulegone or menthol. As with almost any plant, nibbling the leaves can cause mild, short-lived stomach upset. Take care not to confuse it with lemon-scented true mints (Mentha spp.); true mint essential oils, especially pennyroyal, are toxic to cats.
safetyNotes: Not listed as toxic to cats by the ASPCA; Monarda species are widely regarded as non-toxic to pets
Aromatic oils are dominated by thymol, p-cymene, and carvacrol; the plant does not contain pulegone or menthol (pulegone is the toxic principle of pennyroyal, Mentha pulegium — a different plant)
Nibbling fresh leaves may cause mild, self-limiting stomach upset or drooling, as with many plants
Keep concentrated essential oils of any aromatic herb away from cats
Do not confuse Lemon Mint (Monarda citriodora) with lemon-scented true mints (Mentha spp.), which are toxic to cats
